title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Laboratory testing is central to diagnostic evaluation, yet errors can occur during the preanalytical, analytical, and postanalytical phases. These errors produce inaccurate or delayed results, compromising clinical judgment, increasing resource use, and elevating patient risk. Contributing factors include improper patient preparation, specimen collection errors, transport delays, instrument malfunction, reagent instability, transcription mistakes, and inadequate communication of critical values.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Introduction
content: The laboratory medicine service in a hospital addresses relevant investigations of patients’ presenting complaints and, in some cases, the detection and prevention of disease. The process includes a clinical request for a specific investigation, specimen analysis, result interpretation, and timely reporting. These functions occur within a designated area of the hospital, the pathology laboratory, supervised by a physician specialized in pathology. The pathologist issues reports and guides physician colleagues on optimal utilization of laboratory services. Laboratory size and facilities depend on hospital bed capacity, the population served, and the diversity of cases encountered. [1] [2]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Etiology and Epidemiology
content: Laboratory investigations play a pivotal role in disease diagnosis and management. The number of tests ordered daily increases with the number and complexity of discharge diagnoses. Patients with a single diagnosis underwent an average of 7.5 tests per day. A study reported a daily average of 9.5 tests in the internal medicine department. Similar findings were observed in an American hospital, with an average of 9.67 tests per inpatient day. The average for complete blood count (CBC), a frequently ordered initial test, was 1.07 per day. The most commonly ordered analytes were serum electrolytes, particularly sodium. [3] [4]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Blood Specimens
content: Following patient identification, blood is collected by a phlebotomist from a suitable vein, with the antecubital fossa preferred, using a sterile syringe. The specimen is transferred into properly labeled containers. Blood should clot before processing for serological testing. During transport, the sample must be protected from extreme temperatures. For long-term storage or delayed transport, specimens should be frozen at –20 °C or lower. Serum designated for prompt serological testing should be stored at 2 °C to 8 °C until examination. [5]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Blood Specimens
content: For blood cultures, the laboratory should be contacted to determine the appropriate culture media based on suspected pathogens. The syringe needle must be changed before inoculating the culture bottle to minimize contamination. The rubber bung of the bottle should be cleaned with iodine solution before and after blood injection. The volume of blood inoculated should generally be approximately 10% of the culture medium (eg, 3 mL of blood into 30 mL of medium). Specimens for culture should be collected, whenever possible, prior to initiating antimicrobial therapy.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Throat and Nasal Swabs
content: Swabs are collected under direct visibility and adequate lighting. Preferred sites include areas of exudation, inflammatory membranes, or tonsillar crypts. For nasal specimens, the patient should be seated with the head slightly tilted backward, facing the light source. Insert and rotate the swab repeatedly within 1 nasal cavity. Spread the isolate evenly on 2 to 3 smears, air-dry the slides, and send them to the laboratory for examination. [8]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Sputum Specimens
content: For diseases such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( M. tuberculosis ), a series of 3 early morning specimens, 8 to 10 mL each, should be collected and stored in a refrigerator. In uncooperative patients, M. tuberculosis may be recovered from gastric contents via stomach aspiration. [9]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Fecal Samples
content: Fecal specimens should be collected directly into a clean, dry container with a tightly fitted lid and then transferred to a properly labeled transport container. The specimen should ideally include portions containing visible abnormal material, such as pus, mucus, or blood, and represent the 1st, middle, and last parts of the stool to ensure diagnostic accuracy.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Fecal Samples
content: For suspected cholera, approximately 1 mL (10%) of stool should be inoculated into 10 mL of alkaline peptone water for enrichment. For suspected viral infections, about 1 mL of feces should be mixed with 9 mL of sterile buffered saline and centrifuged for 30 minutes. The supernatant should then be frozen and stored below –40 °C until testing. [10]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Fecal Samples
content: Physical examination of feces includes assessment of color, odor, consistency, parasites, and pH. Microscopic evaluation may reveal food residues, muscle fibers, fats, fatty acid crystals, starch, cellulose, cells (eg, erythrocytes, leukocytes, epithelial cells), crystals (eg, triple phosphate, calcium oxalate, cholesterol), ova and cysts of parasites, motile amoeba (with ingested erythrocytes and pseudopodia), mucus, and foreign bodies (eg, hair, wool). [11] [12]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Urine Specimens
content: Patients collecting specimens themselves should receive proper instructions and use a sterile container. An uncontaminated midstream urine sample provides optimal accuracy for reporting. Physical evaluation includes assessment of volume, odor, color, appearance, pH, and specific gravity. [13] Chemical examination determines the presence and quantity of normal and abnormal elements, including proteins, glucose, reducing sugars, bile pigments (bilirubin), bile salts, blood, nitrites, ketone bodies, urobilinogen, and Bence Jones proteins. [14]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Urine Specimens
content: Microscopic examination is a key component of urinalysis, capable of detecting ova, parasites, red blood cells (RBCs), leukocytes, casts, epithelial cells, and crystals. Additional structures visible under light microscopy include malignant cells, bacteria, yeast, Trichomonas , filaria, spermatozoa, and artifacts such as mucous threads or fat. [15] Automated analyzers, such as Clinitek 100 and Urilux, are used for routine urinalysis, providing accuracy, reducing reliance on subjective visual interpretation, enabling computerized result processing, and minimizing the need for repeat testing. [16]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Body Fluid Samples
content: Pleural, peritoneal, synovial, and pericardial fluids are aspirated aseptically into sterile containers. Appearance, including color, turbidity, viscosity, and presence of clots, should be recorded. Portions are allocated for cell count and differential, protein and glucose estimation, and microbiologic culture. Cytological examination aids in detecting malignant cells. For microbiologic culture, samples should be transported promptly at room temperature to maintain organism viability. [17]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Tissue and Biopsy Specimens
content: Biopsy or surgical tissue samples for microbiological or histopathological examination should be collected aseptically in sterile, leak-proof containers. For histopathology, tissues are preserved in 10% neutral buffered formalin. For microbiology or molecular testing, specimens should remain sterile and refrigerated at 2 °C to 8 °C, unless freezing is specifically required. Proper labeling and documentation are essential for traceability and accurate interpretation. [18]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Cerebrospinal Fluid Samples
content: Cerebrospinal fluid is collected by lumbar puncture under strict aseptic precautions, typically between the L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspaces. The specimen is distributed into 3 sterile tubes, designated for different analyses: tube 1 for chemistry and serology, tube 2 for microbiological culture and sensitivity, and tube 3 for cytological examination. Immediate processing is essential, as delays can cause cellular degeneration and alter biochemical parameters, particularly glucose concentration. [19]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure -- Cerebrospinal Fluid Samples
content: Cerebrospinal fluid must not be refrigerated for microbiological studies, as low temperatures can reduce the viability of pathogens such as Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae . Specimens should be maintained at room temperature or in an incubator enriched with carbon dioxide until examination. Proper handling and prompt analysis ensure reliable diagnostic results and prevent false-negative findings in critical neurological and infectious conditions. [20]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests
content: Physicians order hundreds of laboratory tests to support diagnoses, monitoring, and prognosis of various diseases. The discussion below focuses on the most commonly reported test groups.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests -- Complete Blood Count
content: Common CBC parameters include the RBC count, hemoglobin concentration, hematocrit, and indices that describe RBC size and hemoglobin content. The RBC count reflects the number of erythrocytes per unit volume of blood, with normal ranges of 4.7 to 6.1 million cells/µL in men and 4.2 to 5.4 million cells/µL in women. Hemoglobin indicates the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity, normally 130 to 180 g/L in men and 120 to 160 g/L in women.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests -- Complete Blood Count
content: Hematocrit, representing the proportion of whole blood occupied by packed RBCs, ranges from 45% to 62% in men and 37% to 48% in women. Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) measures RBC size, typically 80 to 100 fL, while mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) quantifies hemoglobin content per cell, 27 to 31 pg. Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), reflecting average hemoglobin concentration within RBCs, ranges from 32% to 36%. Reticulocytes, immature erythrocytes in circulation, normally comprise approximately 1% of the total RBC count.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests -- Complete Blood Count
content: The white blood cell (WBC) count quantifies the number of leukocytes per unit volume of blood, with a normal reference range of approximately 4.3 to 11.0 × 10^9/L. The WBC differential provides the relative and absolute counts of specific leukocyte types, aiding in the assessment of immune status and detection of infections or hematologic disorders. The normal ranges for each cell type are as follows: Neutrophils: 1.8 to 7.8 × 10³/mm³ Lymphocytes: 0.7 to 4.5 × 10³/mm³ Monocytes: 0.1 to 1.0 × 10³/mm³ Eosinophils: 0 to 0.4 × 10³/mm³ Basophils: 0 to 0.2 × 10³/mm³

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests -- Complete Blood Count
content: The platelet count quantifies the number of platelets per unit volume of blood, with a normal range of 150 to 400 × 10³/µL. Thrombocytopenia, characterized by a low platelet count, may be primary, occurring in isolation without an identifiable underlying cause, or secondary, developing alongside conditions such as HIV, hepatitis C virus, systemic lupus erythematosus, or chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Drug-induced thrombocytopenia can also arise from the use of agents like aspirin, ethanol, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

content: A peripheral smear examines the size, shape, color, count, and composition of blood cells, including the presence of inclusions, compared with normal morphology. This test is typically performed when abnormalities are detected on a CBC or clinical suspicion exists for hematologic disorders such as anemia, leukemia, or platelet abnormalities.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests -- Modalities for Evaluating Hemostasis
content: Prothrombin time, reported alongside laboratory control with a normal range of 11 to 24 seconds, assesses the extrinsic coagulation pathway, specifically factor VII, as well as the common pathway. Prolongation occurs with vitamin K or factor VII deficiency and with therapy using vitamin K antagonists, such as warfarin. The international normalized ratio (INR) has a normal range of 0.9 to 1.2. This parameter standardizes prothrombin time results and is used to monitor warfarin therapy and evaluate hepatic function.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests -- Modalities for Evaluating Hemostasis
content: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), measured against a normal control with a reference range of 22 to 35 seconds, evaluates the activity of the intrinsic and common pathways, including factors VIII, IX, XI, and XII. This test is also employed to monitor heparin therapy and is prolonged in hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and B (factor IX deficiency).

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests -- Diagnostic Tests in Diabetes Mellitus
content: Diagnosis and monitoring of diabetes mellitus rely on quantitative laboratory assessments of blood glucose and long-term glycemic control. Fasting blood glucose (FBG) measures circulating glucose after an overnight fast, with a normal value of less than 100 mg/dL. Random blood glucose (RBG), obtained irrespective of the last meal, is considered normal below 140 mg/dL.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests -- Diagnostic Tests in Diabetes Mellitus
content: Glycosylated hemoglobin, or HbA1c, reflects average blood glucose levels over the preceding 2 to 3 months, with a normal value below 5.7%. The 2-hour 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) evaluates the body’s ability to regulate glucose following a standardized glucose load, with a normal postload value below 140 mg/dL. These tests collectively provide essential information for diagnosing diabetes mellitus, guiding therapeutic interventions, and monitoring glycemic control to reduce the risk of acute and chronic complications.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Diagnostic Tests -- Laboratory Investigations in Hepatobiliary Disease
content: The following laboratory tests are commonly ordered to evaluate liver function and detect hepatocellular injury. title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures
content: The preanalytical phase involves proper preparation of materials, sterilization and disinfection of equipment, and strict adherence to aseptic techniques to maintain specimen integrity and prevent contamination. The analytical phase encompasses the selection and application of appropriate testing methodologies, including titration, electrophoresis, chromatography, molecular techniques, and optical or physical methods, to generate precise and reliable results. The postanalytical phase focuses on verification, interpretation, documentation, and communication of results to support meaningful clinical decision-making. Together, these phases ensure precision, reliability, and reproducibility throughout the entire testing cycle.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Sterilization and Disinfection
content: Microbiological and biochemical testing requires the use of sterile culture media, containers, and instruments free from all contaminating microorganisms. Sterilization denotes the complete elimination of all forms of microbial life, including bacteria, spores, fungi, and viruses, whether pathogenic or nonpathogenic. This procedure is applied to culture media, reagents, containers, and laboratory equipment to maintain contamination-free conditions. [21]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Sterilization and Disinfection
content: Several methods achieve sterilization, including heat, radiation, filtration, and chemical disinfection. Heat sterilization may be performed using dry or moist heat, with the autoclave being the most commonly employed apparatus. During autoclaving, items are exposed to pressurized steam at 121 °C, which denatures proteins and destroys spores and vegetative cells. This method effectively sterilizes culture media, surgical instruments, and laboratory linen. Autoclave efficiency is verified using chemical indicators, such as the Browne tube or Bowie-Dick tape, and biological indicators, including spores of Bacillus stearothermophilus . [22]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Sterilization and Disinfection
content: Filtration is another sterilization method employed for heat-sensitive materials, such as antisera, toxins, or enzyme solutions. Filtration techniques are classified as surface filtration, in which particles are retained on the filter surface, and depth filtration, in which particles are trapped within the filter matrix. Common materials include membrane filters, sintered glass, asbestos pads, and ceramic filters. [23]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Sterilization and Disinfection
content: Disinfection, distinct from sterilization, refers to the destruction of most vegetative microorganisms but does not necessarily eliminate spores. Disinfectants act by disrupting proteins, lipids, or nucleic acids within microbial cells. Antiseptics are mild disinfectants suitable for application on living tissues (eg, alcohol, povidone-iodine, spirit), whereas disinfectants are more concentrated and corrosive, intended for use on inanimate objects (eg, phenol, Lysol, chlorine, formaldehyde, mercuric chloride). [24] Proper application of sterilization and disinfection procedures is essential to ensure the validity, reliability, and safety of all subsequent laboratory analyses.

Each method provides different types of information, allowing clinicians to evaluate physiological states, monitor disease progression, and guide therapeutic decisions.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Titration
content: Titration is a fundamental quantitative analytical method for determining the concentration of an acid or base in a solution through a neutralization reaction, typically using an indicator to identify the endpoint. In clinical laboratory testing, titration is employed to measure acid and base levels in body fluids, such as gastric juice or urine, providing diagnostic information on acid-base balance. [25]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Electrophoresis
content: Electrophoresis separates charged molecules based on their mobility in an electric field, with positively charged ions migrating toward the cathode and negatively charged ions toward the anode. This technique is extensively applied for protein fractionation, hemoglobin variant detection, and lipoprotein or isoenzyme analysis. Electrophoresis yields both qualitative and quantitative data essential for diagnosing and monitoring disorders such as multiple myeloma, hemoglobinopathies, and dyslipidemias. [26]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Chromatography
content: Chromatography separates components of a mixture according to their differential movement through stationary and mobile phases. Common methods include column, thin-layer, and liquid chromatography, as well as high-performance liquid chromatography. These techniques are widely used to identify and quantify drugs, metabolites, toxic compounds, amino acids, hormones, and carbohydrates, providing high specificity and serving a critical role in clinical and toxicological testing. [27]

Common amplification methods include polymerase chain reaction (PCR), ligase chain reaction (LCR), nucleic acid-based amplification (NASBA), and strand displacement assays (SDA).

content: Various optical and physical methods are used to detect, quantify, and characterize substances in clinical specimens. Different techniques offer complementary advantages in sensitivity, specificity, and applicability, enabling accurate assessment across multiple analytes and sample types.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Spectrophotometry
content: Spectrophotometry is a fundamental and widely applied optical method in the laboratory. The technique measures light absorbance by a colored or color-producing solution at a specific wavelength, based on the principle that absorbance is directly proportional to analyte concentration, enabling precise quantitative determination. [29] Spectrophotometric methods are routinely applied to assess substances such as glucose, urea, creatinine, and bilirubin, as well as enzyme activity. Ultraviolet (180–400 nm) and visible (400–700 nm) spectrophotometry accommodate a wide range of biological specimens, including serum, plasma, and urine. [30]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Atomic absorption spectrometry
content: Atomic absorption spectrometry (AAS) measures light absorption by free atoms in the gaseous state. The technique demonstrates high specificity and sensitivity for trace and ultratrace metal analysis, including calcium, magnesium, zinc, copper, and lead. Each element absorbs light at characteristic wavelengths, enabling precise quantification. [31] Two principal techniques exist: flame AAS, which atomizes samples in a flame for higher analyte concentrations, and graphite furnace AAS, which increases sensitivity for low-concentration samples by electrically vaporizing the sample in a graphite tube. AAS remains a cornerstone for trace metal analysis in clinical and toxicological laboratories. [32]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Fluorometry
content: Fluorometry, or fluorescence spectroscopy, measures light emitted by a substance following excitation at a specific wavelength. Emitted fluorescence is directly proportional to analyte concentration, allowing highly sensitive quantification, often up to a thousand times more sensitive than spectrophotometry. Applications include hormone assays, enzyme kinetics, and therapeutic drug monitoring. Specificity is enhanced by selecting excitation and emission wavelengths unique to the fluorescent compound or complex generated during the reaction. [33]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Chemiluminescence
content: Chemiluminescence relies on light emission generated by a chemical reaction rather than excitation from an external light source. Light intensity correlates directly with analyte or reaction product concentration. This method is extensively applied in immunoassays, including assays for cardiac troponins and hormones like thyroid-stimulating hormone, due to its high sensitivity, broad dynamic range, and minimal background interference. Modern automated analyzers incorporate chemiluminescent detection systems, enabling high-throughput testing with excellent precision. [34] [35]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Nephelometry and turbidimetry
content: Nephelometry and turbidimetry assess light scattering caused by particles suspended in liquid samples, such as proteins or immune complexes. Turbidimetry quantifies the decrease in transmitted light intensity as light passes through the sample, whereas nephelometry measures light scattered at a defined angle relative to the incident beam. Nephelometry offers greater sensitivity and is preferred for quantitative determination of plasma proteins, including C-reactive protein, immunoglobulins, and complement components. Both methods are widely employed in immunological and protein assays where particle formation forms part of the analytical reaction. [36]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Refractometry
content: Refractometry measures the refractive index of a solution, which varies with solute concentration. This rapid and straightforward technique is used in clinical laboratories to determine urine specific gravity and estimate total plasma protein concentration. The method is based on Snell’s law, describing the bending of light as it passes between media of differing refractive indices. Despite having lower sensitivity than other optical methods, refractometry provides valuable, rapid screening data in routine urinalysis and plasma studies. [37]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Testing Procedures -- Polarimetry
content: Polarimetry quantifies the rotation of plane-polarized light by optically active (chiral) compounds. Rotation magnitude depends on sample concentration, optical path length, and the compound’s specific rotation. The method is particularly effective for quantitative analysis of carbohydrates, such as glucose, and for assessing the optical purity of enantiomeric substances. In clinical chemistry, polarimetry holds historical importance in glucose analysis and remains a teaching tool for understanding optical activity in biochemical compounds. [38]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Interfering Factors
content: Before ordering any laboratory test, clinicians must follow a logical, clinically sound approach to ensure that testing is appropriate, meaningful, and beneficial to patient care. Tests should be relevant to the diagnostic hypothesis, directly addressing the patient’s clinical problem. Timing and necessity require consideration of whether changes in the patient’s condition justify performing or repeating the test, with repeat testing reserved for situations likely to yield new or useful information. The potential impact on management must be evaluated, including confirmation of diagnosis, guidance of therapy, or monitoring of treatment response.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Approach to Complete Blood Count Interpretation
content: Understanding hematopoiesis is essential to interpreting a CBC accurately. Hemopoiesis encompasses the formation of mature blood cells from immature precursors and involves a series of distinctively recognizable stages. Production of RBCs, WBCs, platelets, and lymphocytes is termed "erythropoiesis," "granulopoiesis," "thrombopoiesis," and "lymphopoiesis," respectively. A dynamic balance exists between cell production and destruction, with each cell type maintaining a normal range in circulating blood. [40]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Approach to Complete Blood Count Interpretation
content: Concurrent decreases in RBCs and platelets suggest a consumptive or destructive process in the peripheral blood. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemias, including thrombotic microangiopathies such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and hemolytic uremic syndrome, comprise a key group of disorders producing this pattern. [42] [43] Isolated abnormalities in a single cell line direct evaluation toward that lineage. Reduced RBCs indicate anemia, prompting assessment for causes such as blood loss, hemolysis, or impaired production. A marked elevation in WBCs with immature forms raises suspicion for leukemia or a leukemoid reaction. Involvement of multiple cell lines points toward bone marrow disorders, including aplastic anemia or myelodysplastic syndrome. [44]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Anemias
content: Anemia is defined as a reduction in hemoglobin concentration or total circulating red cell mass below the reference interval for an individual’s age and sex. Common clinical manifestations include fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, palpitations, dizziness, headache, and decreased exercise tolerance. [45] Initial diagnostic evaluation for suspected anemia typically includes a CBC with differential, reticulocyte count, and peripheral blood smear.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Anemias
content: Morphologically, anemias are classified into 3 major types. Microcytic hypochromic anemia is characterized by smaller-than-normal RBCs with reduced hemoglobin content, as seen in iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia, and anemia of chronic disease. Macrocytic anemia involves larger-than-normal RBCs, with hemoglobin concentration that may be normal or reduced, occurring in vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, exposure to certain drugs, alcoholism, liver disease, and hypothyroidism. Normocytic normochromic anemia features RBCs of normal size but reduced hemoglobin concentration, as observed in acute blood loss, leukemias, bone marrow infiltration, chronic renal failure, and chronic infections.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Leukemias
content: Leukemia is a hematological malignancy characterized by uncontrolled proliferation, abnormal maturation, and accumulation of immature or intermediate blood cells. Classification into acute and chronic forms depends on the rate of disease progression and the maturation stage of malignant cells in the blood and bone marrow. [46]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Leukemias
content: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a rapidly progressive malignancy in which myeloid cells fail to differentiate beyond the blast stage. Peripheral blood films typically reveal circulating blasts with Auer rods, representing azurophilic granules. [47] Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) involves increased proliferation of the granulocytic lineage without loss of differentiation capacity. Peripheral blood films show a leukoerythroblastic picture with predominance of immature red cells and granulocytes. Detection of the BCR-ABL fusion gene confirms the diagnosis in over 90% of cases.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Leukemias
content: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) arises from the proliferation of early lymphoid precursor cells, which replace normal progenitor cells in the bone marrow. Leukemic lymphoblasts lack distinctive morphological features, making immunophenotyping essential for diagnosis. Cytogenetic analysis demonstrates the Philadelphia chromosome in approximately 25% of adult cases. [48] Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a clonal malignancy of mature B cells. CBC reveals a B-lymphocyte population exceeding 5 × 10/L, while peripheral blood films show small mature lymphocytes and numerous smudge cells. [49]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Diagnostic Approach to Coagulation Abnormalities
content: Suspected coagulation disorder cases warrant a carefully planned diagnostic strategy. A thorough history and physical examination are critical, as they help distinguish between vascular defects, platelet disorders, and deficiencies or dysfunctions of coagulation factors. Clinical findings may also indicate whether the disorder is hereditary or acquired, guiding the selection of appropriate laboratory tests. Initial screening generally includes platelet count, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time. The results of these preliminary investigations direct further diagnostic testing. title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Laboratory-Based Approach to Suspected Diabetes Mellitus
content: Diabetes mellitus is a metabolic disorder marked by hyperglycemia and associated disturbances in carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism, arising from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both. Common clinical manifestations include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, unintentional weight loss, blurred vision, and increased susceptibility to infections. [51] Diabetes mellitus is broadly classified into 2 major types: type 1 diabetes mellitus, which may be immune-mediated or idiopathic, and type 2 diabetes mellitus, which is primarily associated with insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency, often linked to obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and genetic predisposition. Any one of the following is diagnostic: FBG of at least 126 mg/dL, or 2-hour OGTT greater than or equal to 200 mg/dL, or RBG no less than 200 mg/dL along with classic symptoms of diabetes mellitus, or HbA1c above or equal to 6.5%

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Analysis and Interpretation of Liver Function Markers
content: Increased prothrombin time, international normalized ratio, and serum direct bilirubin, as well as disproportionate elevation of ALT or AST and reduced serum albumin, collectively point to hepatocellular dysfunction. ALT is more specific for hepatocellular injury, whereas AST is present in multiple tissues, including skeletal and cardiac muscle. An AST-to-ALT ratio greater than 2:1 suggests alcoholic liver disease. [53]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Laboratory Assessment of Kidney Function
content: The interpretation of renal function tests requires assessment of markers reflecting glomerular filtration, tubular function, and overall kidney integrity. Serum creatinine is the most commonly used indicator of renal function, though it is influenced by factors such as muscle mass, age, and hydration status. An elevation in serum creatinine typically signifies a reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which may result from acute kidney injury or chronic kidney disease. [56]

content: Blood urea nitrogen also reflects renal function but is less specific, as it is affected by protein intake, liver function, and hydration status. A blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine ratio greater than 20:1 suggests a prerenal cause, such as dehydration or reduced renal perfusion. Estimated GFR (eGFR), calculated using creatinine-based equations, provides a more accurate assessment of renal function over time and is useful for staging chronic kidney disease. [57]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings -- Integrating Electrolyte Results with Clinical Context
content: Accurate interpretation of electrolyte results requires integrating serum concentrations with the patient’s clinical status, fluid balance, acid-base state, and renal function. Sodium primarily reflects water balance rather than total body sodium. Therefore, hyponatremia and hypernatremia must be interpreted in the context of volume status—hypovolemic, euvolemic, or hypervolemic—as each pattern indicates different underlying mechanisms, including dehydration, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), or heart failure. [59]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Clinical Significance
content: Laboratory tests provide clinical value when they support the timely detection, diagnosis, and monitoring of disease. Testing without a clear clinical justification or interpretation in the appropriate clinical context carries risk. Unnecessary or excessive testing may lead to repeated phlebotomies that cause phlebitis, pain, or bruising, and may also delay essential diagnostic procedures. Inappropriate test utilization wastes patient and laboratory personnel time, increases healthcare costs, and creates diagnostic confusion or anxiety due to false-positive results. Optimal test use requires sound clinical evaluation, appropriate test selection, and periodic reassessment of the necessity and frequency of laboratory monitoring.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Clinical Significance
content: The “Choosing Wisely” campaign of the American Board of Internal Medicine promotes the selection of clinically valuable tests and encourages clinicians and patients to use laboratory resources judiciously. Laboratory testing accounts for less than 5% of healthcare spending yet influences approximately 70% of major decisions regarding admission, treatment, and discharge. Studies based on clinical guideline recommendations show that 25% to 30% of repeat testing is unnecessary. Among medical specialties, family medicine practitioners order the highest volume of laboratory tests, followed by internal medicine providers. [63] [64] [65]

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Quality Control and Lab Safety
content: Internal quality control consists of daily checks performed by laboratory staff to confirm that all procedures and equipment consistently deliver accurate and precise results. The process minimizes analytical variability and protects the quality of all reported values. The methods involved are explained below.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Quality Control and Lab Safety -- Levy-Jennings charts
content: Levy-Jennings charts assess both accuracy and precision. Serial daily control measurements are used to calculate the mean and standard deviation (SD), after which results are plotted on graph paper with horizontal lines representing the mean, ±1 SD, ±2 SD, and ±3 SD. Normal and abnormal control values are charted and monitored daily using Westgard rules.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Quality Control and Lab Safety -- 5-Cycle quality control charts
content: Five-cycle charts facilitate daily value recording by running each control 5 consecutive times, generating a broad distribution of results. Horizontal lines are drawn at the mean and ±2 SD from the standard reference. The control is introduced randomly during daily runs, and the mean for that day is calculated and plotted. A consistent rise or fall on one side of the mean indicates an upward or downward trend.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Quality Control and Lab Safety -- Moving 2 standard deviation charts
content: Moving 2 SD charts contain 4 columns, with the leftmost column used to record each day’s deviation from the assigned control mean. For each control run, the mean value for that day is calculated, and the difference from the assigned mean is entered into the corresponding slot. At week’s end, the values are summed and divided by 2 to generate the moving 2 SD value. Weekly 2 SD values should not differ markedly from the assigned 2 SD value for the control.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Quality Control and Lab Safety -- Youden plots
content: These plots compare results from 2 controls. One control is placed on the x-axis and the other on the y-axis. Zero lines connect the axis intersection points and the ±2 SD limits. Approximately 95% of results are expected to fall within the 2 SD squares adjacent to the 0 lines.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Quality Control and Lab Safety -- Results on a patient’s sample
content: A specific patient sample from the previous day is selected and analyzed to assess between-run precision. A mean is calculated from results within a defined range and should remain relatively stable. The values may be displayed graphically. This method is affected by laboratory errors, as well as nonanalytical issues such as sampling and transportation problems.

content: Cumulative sum (CUSUM) charts are applied to daily means or control values. Each day’s SD value is added to or subtracted from the previous cumulative value, producing a cumulative sum chart instead of plotting daily means. A straight line indicates stable accuracy.

content: External quality control evaluates laboratory performance by comparing results across multiple laboratories. Standardized samples are distributed to participating laboratories, and the results are analyzed critically and statistically. This approach allows comparison of different methodologies, identifies interlaboratory variability, and supports the establishment of recommended standard procedures.

title: Overview on Ordering and Evaluation of Laboratory Tests -- Quality Control and Lab Safety -- Laboratory Safety Practices
content: Laboratory safety requires strict adherence to standardized procedures to prevent accidents and contamination. Hands should be thoroughly washed before and after all laboratory activities. Personal protective equipment, including gloves, masks, goggles, and gowns, must be worn when handling reagents and testing materials. Eating, drinking, and smoking are strictly prohibited on laboratory premises, and pipetting by mouth is never permitted.

Operators must acquire appropriate training and proficiency before using unfamiliar equipment or techniques, and caution must be exercised when transferring or mixing chemicals.
